content: In human anatomy, the term hamstring refers to one of the tendons that form the boundaries of the space located behind the knee. In modern anatomical contexts, the term typically refers to the tendons of three specific muscles: the semitendinosus, the semimembranosus, and the biceps femoris. In quadrupeds, the hamstring refers to a single large tendon found behind the knee or a comparable area. In humans, the hamstring is situated along the posterior aspect of the femur. The term ham originally referred to the fat and muscle located behind the knee, while string refers to tendons. Thus, the hamstrings are the string-like tendons that can be palpated on either side of the back of the knee. The four muscles of the posterior thigh are responsible for flexing (bending) the knee, while three of these muscles also extend (straighten) the hip. The short head of the biceps femoris, due to its distinct origin and innervation, does not contribute to hip extension and is sometimes excluded from the definition of the hamstring. The hamstrings act across two joints: the hip and the knee. The semitendinosus and semimembranosus muscles extend the hip when the trunk is fixed or extend the trunk when the hip is fixed. They also flex the knee and medially (inwardly) rotate the lower leg when the knee is bent. The long head of the biceps femoris extends the hip, such as during the initiation of walking. Both the short and long heads of the biceps femoris flex the knee and laterally (outwardly) rotate the lower leg when the knee is bent. The hamstrings play a critical role in various daily activities, including walking, running, jumping, and controlling certain trunk movements. During walking, they function primarily as antagonists to the quadriceps, decelerating knee extension. A hamstring strain, commonly referred to as a pulled hamstring, occurs when there is an excessive stretch or tear of the muscle fibers and associated tissues. Grade I Hamstring Strain: In a grade one hamstring strain, symptoms may not become apparent until after the activity has concluded. The individual may experience a sensation of cramping or tightness, along with mild pain when the muscles are stretched or contracted. This type of injury is sometimes colloquially referred to as a pulled hammy. Grade II Hamstring Strain: A grade two hamstring strain is characterized by immediate pain that is more severe than that of a grade one injury. Pain is confirmed upon stretching or contracting the muscle, and the affected area is typically tender to the touch. Grade III Hamstring Strain: A grade three hamstring strain is a severe injury involving a complete tear of the muscle. It is associated with immediate burning or stabbing pain, and the individual is unable to walk without significant discomfort. A noticeable lump of muscle tissue may form above a depression at the site of the tear. Within a few days, grade two and grade three injuries may result in extensive bruising below the injury site due to bleeding within the tissues. Treatment: The immediate treatment for any muscle injury follows the RICE protocol: rest, ice, compression, and elevation. Ice should never be applied directly to the skin. This approach aims to minimize bleeding and tissue damage. Rest is crucial, although it is often overlooked by competitive athletes. Ignoring rest can exacerbate the injury, potentially worsening a grade one strain to a grade two or a grade two strain to a grade three. As a general guideline, grade one hamstring strains require approximately three weeks of rest from sporting activities, while grade two injuries necessitate four to six weeks. In cases of complete rupture, surgical repair is required, followed by a rehabilitation period of approximately three months. Regardless of the injury's severity, the initial five days of treatment remain consistent. During this time, the hamstring should be rested in an elevated position with an ice pack applied for 20 minutes every two hours, if feasible. A compression bandage should be used to limit bleeding and swelling. After the initial five-day period, more active rehabilitation can commence. Use in Surgery: The distal semitendinosus tendon is one of the tendons that can be utilized in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction surgery. In this procedure, a portion of the tendon is harvested to replace the ACL, which is one of the four major ligaments in the knee.
